mustMemorise: A current in a metal is free electrons drifting between metal atoms held in fixed positions
The electrons collide with the atoms: that is resistance, and it transfers energy as heat
Heating: electrons collide with atoms, the atoms vibrate more, the wire gets hotter
Resistance is directly proportional to length (same wire, constant temperature)
The graph of resistance (y) against length (x) is a straight line through the origin
Independent: length. Dependent: resistance. Controls: thickness, material, temperature
Ammeter in series, voltmeter across the length tested, R = V ÷ I
Gradient = rise ÷ run, in Ω/m: the resistance of one metre

mustBeAbleTo: Explain why a current heats a metal wire: free electrons collide with the metal atoms and transfer energy to them
Name heat (thermal energy) as the main form of energy produced
Explain why a longer wire has a greater resistance, in terms of more collisions
Find the resistance of another length of the same wire by going through one metre
Describe the practical: ammeter in series, voltmeter across the length tested, lengths set on a metre rule, R = V ÷ I
Name the independent, dependent and control variables, and say how the temperature is kept constant
Plot resistance (vertical) against length (horizontal) with a label and unit on each axis and one ruled line
State that resistance is directly proportional to length, from a straight line through the origin
Calculate the gradient, give its unit (Ω/m) and say that it is the resistance of one metre
sheet.howExamined: The practical is set in Unit 7 Physics Booklet B (35 marks in 30 minutes, calculator allowed): completing the circuit with the two meters, naming a control variable, plotting the graph, stating the relationship, and the gradient with its unit. P2 (1 hour 15 minutes) sets the heating effect as a short answer of [3] or [4] (the energy form, the two particles and that they collide), usually followed by a current from P = I × V.
traps: Giving the length as a control variable, when it is the independent variable (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2)
Leaving the unit off the resistance axis, or the axis unlabelled (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2; Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q3)
Describing the relationship in your own words instead of 'directly proportional' (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2)

Writing electrical energy instead of heat as the energy produced (Summer 2025 P2 F Q7; Summer 2023 P2 F Q6)

noteBlocks.lede: Inside a metal wire, free electrons keep bumping into the metal atoms. That one event answers two exam questions: why a longer wire has more resistance, and why a current heats a wire. Then you run the practical that proves the first, from the circuit to the gradient of the graph.

noteBlocks.md: A toaster glows, a kettle element boils water, and a phone charger's cable feels warm after a while. Each one is a metal wire carrying a current. Look inside the wire, and a single event explains both the heat and the wire's resistance.

noteBlocks.caption: Twice the length: twice as many atoms in the way, so twice the collisions.

noteBlocks.md: A metal is made of **atoms** held in fixed positions, with **free electrons** that drift between them; a current is that drift. The electrons keep **colliding with the atoms**. Each collision gets in the way of the flow, and that opposition is the wire's **resistance**. Each collision also hands the atom some energy, which **heats** the wire.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a metal wire carrying a current, what do the free electrons collide with?
options: the metal atoms of the wire
the protons in the atoms' nuclei
the plastic insulation round the wire
noteBlocks.answer: the metal atoms of the wire
noteBlocks.explain: Picture the magnified wire: rows of metal atoms held in place, and electrons zig-zagging between them. Every bump in the electron's path is a whole atom. Protons sit deep inside each atom's nucleus, and the plastic is outside the metal altogether. The answer is the metal atoms of the wire.

noteBlocks.md:
In each collision the electron passes some of its energy to the atom, and the atom **vibrates more**. Atoms vibrating harder is what a hotter wire is. So the energy a current produces in a wire is **heat** (thermal energy).
A full answer names four things: **heat**, the **electrons**, the **atoms**, and that they **collide**.

noteBlocks.title: Where the marks went
noteBlocks.md: **Summer 2025 Foundation:** a surprisingly large share did not give heat as the energy. **Summer 2023:** most named the electrons, but many gave a particle from inside the atom as the other one, and only the more able said the particles collide.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question asks why a kettle element gets hot when a current flows. Which answer names all four things the marks are for?
options: heat is produced because the free electrons collide with the metal atoms
electrical energy is produced as the electrons move through the wire
heat is produced because the electrons collide with the protons
the current is used up in the element and turns into heat
noteBlocks.answer: heat is produced because the free electrons collide with the metal atoms
noteBlocks.explain: Check each answer for the four things: the energy (heat), both particles (electrons and atoms) and what they do (collide). Electrical energy is what goes in, not what comes out; protons are inside the atom's nucleus; and the current is never used up. Only the answer with electrons colliding with the metal atoms has all four.

noteBlocks.md: Twice the length means twice as many atoms in the way, so twice the collisions and **twice the resistance**. For the same wire at a constant temperature, resistance is **directly proportional** to length.

To find the resistance of another length, go through one metre. A 2.0 m length has 8.0 Ω.
**Step 1.** One metre: 8.0 ÷ 2.0 = 4.0 Ω
**Step 2.** 3.5 m: 4.0 × 3.5 = 14 Ω

noteBlocks.title: Why the graph starts at zero
noteBlocks.md: No length means no wire, so no atoms to collide with and no resistance. That is why a graph of resistance against length for one wire is a **straight line through the origin**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A 0.50 m length of a wire has a resistance of 3.0 Ω. What is the resistance of 1.5 m of the same wire, in ohms?
noteBlocks.explain: Go through one metre, as with the pieces of wire: 3.0 ÷ 0.50 = 6.0 Ω for each metre, then 6.0 × 1.5 = 9.0 Ω. A check: 1.5 m is three times 0.50 m, so the resistance is three times 3.0 Ω.

noteBlocks.md: Tape the wire along a metre rule. The **ammeter** goes **in series**, so the current in the wire flows through it. The **voltmeter** goes **across** the length being tested, from the fixed clip to the sliding clip. For each length, read the voltmeter and the ammeter and work out $R = V \div I$. Move the clip and repeat for at least five lengths.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the resistance and length circuit, how is the voltmeter connected?
options: across the length of wire being tested
in series with the wire
across the cells only
noteBlocks.answer: across the length of wire being tested
noteBlocks.explain: Follow the voltmeter's two leads in the circuit: one goes to the fixed clip and one to the sliding clip, so it measures the voltage across exactly the stretch of wire being tested, in parallel with it. It is the ammeter that goes in series, because the current has to flow through it. The answer is across the length being tested.

noteBlocks.md: Name the variables in a fixed order: the one you **change** (independent), the one you **measure** (dependent), then the ones you **keep the same** (controls). With the length written first, it cannot turn up again as a control.

In this practical:
**Changed.** The length: 0.20 m, 0.40 m, 0.60 m, 0.80 m and 1.00 m.
**Measured.** The resistance at each length, from R = V ÷ I.
**Kept the same.** The thickness and the material (one wire along the 1.00 m rule) and the temperature.

noteBlocks.title: Why switch off between readings
noteBlocks.md: A current heats the wire, and a hotter wire has a higher resistance. A small current, switched off between readings, keeps the temperature steady, so only the length changes the resistance.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the resistance and length practical, which of these is a control variable?
options: the thickness of the wire
the length of the wire
the resistance of the wire
noteBlocks.explain: Go through the order again: the length is changed, so it is the independent variable; the resistance is measured, so it is the dependent variable. What is left to keep the same is the thickness, the material and the temperature. Summer 2025 examiners found most candidates wrote the length here. The answer is the thickness of the wire.

noteBlocks.md: The practical booklet (Unit 7, Booklet B) gives you the table and the grid. The graph is worth five marks: a scale that uses at least half the grid, the label **with its unit** on the resistance axis (resistance / Ω), the points, and one ruled straight line of best fit.

Then one mark for the relationship. A straight line through the origin means **directly proportional**, and those two words are the mark. In Summer 2025 most candidates described the trend in their own words instead and scored nothing.

noteBlocks.prompt: A graph of resistance against length for one wire is a straight line through the origin. Give the two-word term for the relationship between resistance and length.
noteBlocks.answer: directly proportional | proportional | resistance is directly proportional to length | resistance is proportional to length | they are directly proportional
noteBlocks.explain: A straight line through the origin means doubling the length doubles the resistance, and the scientific term for that is directly proportional. A sentence such as 'as the length goes up, the resistance goes up' describes a trend but earns nothing, because a curve would fit it too. Write: directly proportional.

noteBlocks.md: A gradient measures how steeply a line climbs: the **rise** (how far up) divided by the **run** (how far across). Here the rise is in ohms and the run in metres, so the gradient is the ohms for each metre: the **resistance of one metre**, in **ohms per metre, Ω/m**.

**Step 1.** gradient = rise ÷ run
**Step 2.** up 4.8 Ω, across 0.80 m
**Step 3.** gradient = 4.8 ÷ 0.80 = 6.0
**Step 4.** ohms up, metres across: **Ω/m**
Check it against the wire: 6.0 Ω/m means each metre has 6.0 Ω. Ω alone, or m/Ω, loses the unit mark; in Summer 2025 a surprising number of Higher candidates did exactly that.

noteBlocks.prompt: Another wire's line rises 7.5 Ω across 1.5 m. What is its gradient, in ohms per metre?
noteBlocks.explain: A gradient is rise ÷ run, as in the four steps: 7.5 ÷ 1.5 = 5.0. The rise is in ohms and the run in metres, so the gradient is 5.0 Ω/m: each metre of that wire has a resistance of 5.0 Ω.

noteBlocks.title: Watching it for CCEA
noteBlocks.md: The video is made for another exam board. If it moves on to resistors in series and in parallel, that is a different CCEA topic, and its 'potential difference' is what CCEA calls voltage. The method for a length of wire is the same as CCEA's.

Watch the order the method runs in: set a length, read the voltmeter and the ammeter, work out the resistance, then move the clip to the next length. A method answer in the exam follows the same order.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the resistance and length practical, which equation turns the voltmeter and ammeter readings into a resistance?
options: R = V ÷ I
R = V × I
R = I ÷ V
noteBlocks.explain: Resistance is how many volts it takes to push each ampere through the wire, so the voltmeter reading is divided by the ammeter reading, both taken at the same length. Summer 2024 examiners saw many start from a wrong version of this and score nothing. The answer is R = V ÷ I.

noteBlocks.md: **Heat opens a longer question.** P2 asks for the energy and how the particles produce it [3–4], then for the appliance's current from P = I × V (Summer 2019, 2023 and 2025). First line: heat; the free electrons collide with the metal atoms.

Both halves, for a 1.38 kW heater on the 230 V mains:
**Energy.** Heat: free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy.
**Convert.** 1.38 kW = 1380 W
**Equation.** P = I × V, so 1380 = I × 230
**Current.** I = 1380 ÷ 230 = 6 A

noteBlocks.prompt: A question says a toaster element gets hot and asks how the particles produce this energy [3]. Which first line earns the most marks?
options: Free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy.
Electrical energy is changed into heat energy in the element.
The element has a high resistance, so it gets hot.
noteBlocks.answer: Free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy.
noteBlocks.explain: Look back at the heater's first line: the marks are for the particles and what they do, so electrons, atoms and collide. A sentence about energy changing form, or about resistance, names no particles and earns none of them. Start with the electrons colliding with the metal atoms, then add that the atoms vibrate more.

noteBlocks.md: **'State the relationship' is one term.** Only 'directly proportional' earns the mark (Summer 2025).
**The unit has its own box.** At Higher the unit gets its own space and its own mark (Summer 2022, Summer 2025): gradient = rise ÷ run, then Ω/m.

**Same wire, a different practical.** Booklet A (Summer 2023) kept one length of wire and changed the current. There the current is the independent variable; the commonest wrong answer was the voltage.

Side by side:
**This topic's.** Changed: the length, 0.20 m to 1.00 m. Measured: the resistance.
**Booklet A's.** Changed: the current, up to 0.50 A. Measured: the voltage. Kept: the length, 1.00 m.

noteBlocks.prompt: A practical keeps one 1.00 m length of nichrome wire, changes the current through it and measures the voltage across it. What is the independent variable?
options: the current in the wire
the voltage across the wire
the length of the wire
noteBlocks.explain: The independent variable is the one changed on purpose, as in Booklet A's line of the side-by-side: here that is the current, set each time. The voltage is what is then read, so it is the dependent variable, and the length stays at 1.00 m, so here it is a control. Summer 2023 examiners found the voltage the commonest wrong answer. The answer is the current in the wire.

noteBlocks.title: PhET: Resistance in a Wire

noteBlocks.task: Leave the top slider and the area slider alone, so the material and the thickness stay the same. Set a length and note the resistance, then double the length and read it again. Then move only the area slider and watch what the thickness does to the resistance.

noteBlocks.title: One slider to read as the material
noteBlocks.md: The simulation shows R = ρL ÷ A and a slider for resistivity, ρ. Resistivity is not on the CCEA specification: read that slider as the material of the wire.

The thickness and the material change the resistance too: a thicker wire of the same metal has a lower resistance. That is exactly why they are control variables. Change either one during the practical and the length is no longer the only thing changing the resistance.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the resistance and length practical, why must the thickness of the wire be kept the same?
options: changing it would also change the resistance
a thicker wire cannot be measured on a metre rule
the thickness is the dependent variable
noteBlocks.answer: changing it would also change the resistance
noteBlocks.explain: The simulation shows it: move the area slider and the resistance changes even with the length fixed. If the thickness changed during the practical, you could not tell how much of the change in resistance came from the length. So it is kept the same: it changes the resistance.

steps.decision: On a graph of resistance against length, the rise is a resistance and the run is a length.
Use a large triangle on the line, here from 0.2 m to 1.0 m, and read where each corner meets the line: 0.6 Ω and 3.0 Ω. A big triangle makes reading errors small.

options: A large triangle makes any reading error a smaller fraction of the value
A large triangle gives a larger gradient
The examiner only accepts triangles that start at the origin
whyMenu.explain: Every line on a graph can be read to about half a small square. On a large triangle that half square is a tiny part of the rise and run, so the gradient comes out closer to the true value. Any triangle on the line gives the same gradient.

steps.decision: The run is the triangle's horizontal side, read on the length axis.
Divide the rise by the run.
The unit is the vertical unit per the horizontal unit. It also says what the gradient is: the resistance of one metre of this wire.

twin.stem:
A second wire's line passes through (0.2 m, 1.1 Ω) and (1.0 m, 5.5 Ω).
Calculate its gradient. [3]

workedExamples.stem:
At a length of 0.50 m, the voltmeter reads 1.5 V and the ammeter reads 0.25 A.
(a) Calculate the resistance of this length of wire. (b) Calculate the resistance of 1.2 m of the same wire. [5]

steps.decision: The meters give a voltage and a current; the resistance is the voltage divided by the current.
Substitute the two readings from the same length.
Resistance is proportional to length, so go through one metre first.

options: Because resistance is proportional to length, so each metre of this wire has the same resistance
Because the answer must always be given per metre
Because the voltmeter only reads across one metre
whyMenu.explain: Every metre of one wire has the same number of atoms in the way, so the same resistance. Find that one-metre value, then multiply by any length: 12 Ω for each metre here.

steps.decision: Then scale up to the new length.

twin.stem:
At 0.40 m the voltmeter reads 1.8 V and the ammeter 0.30 A.
Calculate the resistance of 1.0 m of the same wire. [4]

items.stem: Something from the topic before, which this one builds on: a component has 6 V across it and 2 A through it. What is its resistance?

options.feedback: R = V ÷ I = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 Ω. You will use this in the practical.
That multiplies the voltage and the current. Resistance is voltage divided by current: R = V ÷ I.
That is current ÷ voltage. Resistance is voltage ÷ current: R = V ÷ I.

items.stem: Which meter measures the current through a wire, and how is it connected?

options.feedback: The ammeter goes in series, so the current flows through it.
A voltmeter measures voltage, and it goes across a component. Current needs an ammeter in series.
The ammeter is the right meter, but it goes in series so the current passes through it.

items.stem: What does a straight-line graph through the origin tell you about the two quantities?

options.feedback: A straight line through the origin is the picture of direct proportion: double one and the other doubles.
Inverse proportion is a curve: as one goes up, the other goes down. A straight line through the origin is direct proportion.
A straight line through the origin shows a very definite relationship: double one and the other doubles, which is direct proportion.

items.stem: A wire is replaced by one twice as long, of the same material and thickness, at the same temperature. What happens to the resistance?

options.feedback: Twice the length means twice as many atoms in the way, so twice the collisions and twice the resistance.
A longer wire has more atoms in the way, so the resistance goes up, not down: twice the length, twice the resistance.
The material and thickness are the same, but the length is not. More length means more collisions and more resistance: it doubles.

options.text: it is four times as big
options.feedback: Resistance is directly proportional to length, not to length squared: double the length, double the resistance.

items.stem: Why does a metal wire get hot when a current flows through it?

options.text: the free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy
options.feedback: The atoms vibrate more, and atoms vibrating more is a higher temperature.

options.text: the free electrons collide with the protons in the atoms' nuclei
options.feedback: The electrons collide with whole metal atoms, held in place in the wire, not with particles inside the nucleus.

options.text: the current is used up and turns into heat
options.feedback: The current is not used up; the same charge flows all the way round. It is the electrons' collisions with the atoms that pass on energy as heat.

items.stem: In the resistance and length practical, which of these is a control variable?

options.feedback: It is kept the same so that only the length changes the resistance.
The length is the independent variable, the one you change. It cannot be kept the same as well.
The resistance is the dependent variable: the one you measure.

items.stem: A graph of resistance (Ω) against length (m) has a gradient of 5. What is the unit of the gradient?

options.feedback: The vertical unit per the horizontal unit: ohms per metre. It is the resistance of one metre.
Ohms is the vertical axis's unit alone. A gradient divides it by the horizontal unit: Ω/m.
That is upside down. The gradient is rise ÷ run, so the vertical unit, Ω, goes on top: Ω/m.

items.stem: A graph of resistance against length is a straight line through the origin. Which answer earns the mark for 'State the relationship'?

options.text: resistance is directly proportional to length
options.feedback: That is the term the mark is for: a straight line through the origin means directly proportional.

options.text: as the length increases, the resistance increases
options.feedback: True, but it is a trend in your own words, and it would also describe a curve or a line that misses the origin. The mark needs 'directly proportional'.
Correlation describes scattered data. A straight line through the origin is described by one term: directly proportional.

context.setting: The two kinds of particle inside a metal wire

parts.stem: Name the particles that move through a metal wire to carry an electric current.
hints: They are free to drift between the atoms, and they carry a negative charge.
parts.workedSolution: Free electrons. They are free to drift between the metal atoms, and that drift is the current.

parts.stem: As they move, these particles keep colliding with other particles in the wire. Name those other particles.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2023 examiners found most candidates named the electron, but many named a particle from inside the atom for the other.

hints: They are much bigger than an electron and are held in place in the metal.
parts.workedSolution: The metal atoms of the wire (strictly, positive metal ions), which stay in place while the electrons drift past.

commonErrors.feedback: The other particle is the whole metal atom, held in place in the wire, not a particle from inside its nucleus. The free electrons drift between the atoms and collide with them. Summer 2023 examiners saw many answers lose this mark by naming a particle from inside the atom.

context.setting: The element inside an electric kettle

parts.stem:
When a current flows through the metal element of a kettle, electrical energy is changed into another form.
Name the main form of energy produced in the element.
hints: The whole point of a kettle element is that it gets hot.
parts.workedSolution: Heat (thermal energy). The element gets hot and heats the water.

commonErrors.feedback: Electrical energy is what goes into the wire; the question asks what it becomes. The collisions make the metal atoms vibrate more, and that is heat (thermal energy). Summer 2025 and Summer 2023 examiners both saw this mark lost to the word electrical.

parts.stem: Describe how the particles in the element produce this energy.

accepted: the free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy, so the atoms vibrate more and the element heats up
electrons bump into the atoms of the metal and transfer energy to them

hints: Name both kinds of particle, and say what happens when they meet.
parts.workedSolution: The free electrons that carry the current collide with the metal atoms. In each collision an electron gives some of its energy to an atom, so the atoms vibrate more and the element heats up.

commonErrors.feedback: The other particle is the whole metal atom, held in place in the wire, not a particle from inside its nucleus. The free electrons drift between the atoms and collide with them. Summer 2023 examiners saw many answers lose this mark by naming a particle from inside the atom.

context.setting: Offcuts from a reel of nichrome heating wire

parts.stem:
A 2.5 m length of nichrome wire has a resistance of 8.0 Ω.
Calculate the resistance of 1.0 m of the same wire.
hints: Resistance is proportional to length, so share the resistance equally between the metres: divide by the number of metres.
parts.workedSolution: Resistance is proportional to length, so 1.0 m has 8.0 ÷ 2.5 = 3.2 Ω.

parts.stem: Calculate the resistance of 4.0 m of the same wire.
hints: Use your answer for 1.0 m, and multiply by the new length.
parts.workedSolution: Each metre has 3.2 Ω, so 4.0 m has 3.2 × 4.0 = 12.8 Ω.

context.setting: Planning the resistance and length investigation

parts.stem:
A student investigates how changing the length of a wire changes its resistance.
State the independent variable.
hints: The independent variable is the one the student changes on purpose.
parts.workedSolution: The length of the wire: it is the quantity the student changes.

parts.stem: Name one variable the student must keep the same (a control variable).

scheme.for: temperature / material / thickness (diameter, cross-sectional area) of the wire
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Booklet B: naming a control variable was the hardest part of that paper, and most candidates wrote the length.

hints: Not the thing being changed and not the thing being measured: something about the wire itself that must stay the same.
parts.workedSolution: Any one of the thickness of the wire, the material of the wire, or its temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: The length is the independent variable, the one being changed, so it cannot also be kept the same. Name the three in order: length (changed), resistance (measured), then what is left to keep the same: the thickness, the material or the temperature of the wire. parts.stem:
The circuit is used to measure the resistance of different lengths of wire. Meter P is in series with the wire; meter Q is connected across the length being tested.
Choose the name of each meter.

scheme.for: Q: voltmeter (in parallel, across the wire)

hints: A meter in series measures the current flowing through; a meter across a component measures the voltage.
parts.workedSolution: P is the ammeter: it is in series, so the same current flows through it as through the wire. Q is the voltmeter: it is connected across the length being tested, in parallel with it.

commonErrors.feedback: The two meters have been swapped. The ammeter goes in series so the current flows through it; the voltmeter goes across the length of wire, in parallel. Summer 2025 examiners saw many answers put the meters in the wrong places.

parts.stem: Between readings the student switches the current off. Explain why.

accepted: so the wire does not heat up, because a change in temperature would change its resistance
to keep the temperature of the wire constant, since the resistance increases when the wire gets hot

scheme.for: to stop the wire heating up / keep its temperature constant
because the resistance changes (increases) with temperature

hints: A current heats a wire. What does a hotter wire do to its resistance?
parts.workedSolution: So the wire does not heat up. A current heats the wire, and a hotter wire has a higher resistance, so the temperature has to stay constant for the length to be the only thing changing the resistance.

The graph shows the resistance of different lengths of one wire.

parts.workedSolution: Up from 0.60 m to the line, then across: 2.7 Ω.

parts.stem: State the relationship between the resistance of the wire and its length.

accepted: resistance is directly proportional to length

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Booklet B: the term directly proportional was not well recalled, and descriptions in candidates' own words gained nothing.

hints: There is one scientific term for a straight line through the origin.
parts.workedSolution: Resistance is directly proportional to length.

commonErrors.feedback: That describes the trend, but the mark is for the scientific term: resistance is directly proportional to length. A straight line through the origin is what those words mean. Summer 2025 examiners gave nothing for the relationship put in candidates' own words.

parts.stem: Give two features of the graph that show this relationship.

accepted: it is a straight line and it passes through the origin

hints: One feature is about its shape, the other about where it starts.
parts.workedSolution: It is a straight line, and it passes through the origin: zero length has zero resistance.

context.setting: Two pieces cut from the same reel

parts.stem:
Two pieces of wire are cut from the same reel. One is twice as long as the other.
Explain, in terms of particles, why the longer piece has the greater resistance.

accepted: the longer wire has more atoms for the free electrons to pass, so the electrons make more collisions

scheme.for: there are more atoms (ions) in the way / to pass
so the electrons make more collisions (with them)

hints: Think of the electron's journey through the wire. What is there more of in a longer wire?
parts.workedSolution: The longer wire has more atoms for the free electrons to pass, so each electron makes more collisions on its way through. More collisions means more resistance: twice the length, twice the collisions.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the resistance of a wire against its length.
Calculate the gradient of the line on the graph, showing your working.

accept: gradient = change in resistance ÷ change in length

scheme.for: correct substitution from a large triangle, e.g. 4.0 ÷ 1.6

hints: Draw a large triangle on the line and read how far it goes up and how far across.
Gradient = up ÷ across.
parts.workedSolution:
gradient = rise ÷ run
gradient = 4.0 ÷ 1.6
gradient = 2.5
Any large triangle on the line gives the same value.

parts.stem: Give the unit of the gradient.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Booklet B (Higher): most found the gradient, but a surprising number gave the wrong unit for it.

hints: The unit of a gradient is the unit up the side divided by the unit along the bottom.
parts.workedSolution: Ω/m, ohms per metre: the resistance axis is in ohms and the length axis in metres.

commonErrors.feedback: Ohms is the unit of resistance, the vertical axis alone. A gradient is the rise divided by the run, so its unit is the vertical unit divided by the horizontal unit: ohms per metre, Ω/m.
That is the right idea turned upside down. The gradient is rise ÷ run, so the vertical unit goes on top: ohms per metre, Ω/m.

parts.stem: State what the gradient tells you about this wire.

accepted: the resistance of one metre of the wire
the resistance per metre of the wire

scheme.for: the resistance of 1 m of the wire (the resistance per metre)

hints: The gradient is the number of ohms for every metre of length.
parts.workedSolution: It is the resistance of one metre of this wire: the resistance per metre.

parts.stem:
A student measures the resistance of five lengths of one wire. The results are in the table.
Plot the five results on the grid, and draw a straight line of best fit.

scheme.for: three points plotted correctly, each within half a small square
at least four points plotted correctly
one ruled straight line of best fit (through the origin)

hints: Each row of the table is one point: the length across, the resistance up.
Lay one straight line with a ruler; do not join the points dot to dot.
parts.workedSolution: The points are (0.1, 1.6), (0.2, 3.2), (0.3, 4.8), (0.4, 6.4), (0.5, 8.0). They lie on one straight line through the origin, so the line of best fit is ruled from (0, 0) through all five. On the paper the scale and the axis label (resistance / Ω) earn two more marks.

parts.stem: Calculate the gradient of your line.

scheme.for: values from a large triangle on the line, e.g. 8.0 ÷ 0.5

hints: Use the whole line: from the origin to its far end makes the largest triangle.
parts.workedSolution:
gradient = rise ÷ run
gradient = 8.0 ÷ 0.5
gradient = 16

parts.stem: Give the unit of the gradient.
hints: The unit up the side divided by the unit along the bottom.
parts.workedSolution: Ω/m, ohms per metre.

commonErrors.feedback: Ohms alone is the unit of resistance. The gradient divides ohms by metres, so its unit is Ω/m: the resistance of each metre. Summer 2025 Higher examiners saw a surprising number miss this.

context.setting: A toaster: why it gets hot, then the current it draws

parts.stem:
A toaster element is a long metal wire. When the toaster is switched on, the element gets hot.
Name the form of energy produced in the element.
hints: What does the element do to the bread?
parts.workedSolution: Heat (thermal energy).

commonErrors.feedback: Electrical energy is what goes into the wire; the question asks what it becomes. The collisions make the metal atoms vibrate more, and that is heat (thermal energy). Summer 2025 and Summer 2023 examiners both saw this mark lost to the word electrical.

parts.stem: Which two kinds of particle produce this energy, and how do they produce it?

accepted: electrons and atoms: the free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy

hints: One particle moves through the wire; the other is held in place. What happens when they meet?
parts.workedSolution: The electrons and the metal atoms. The free electrons collide with the atoms and give them energy, so the atoms vibrate more and the element heats up.

commonErrors.feedback: The other particle is the whole metal atom, held in place in the wire, not a particle from inside its nucleus. The free electrons drift between the atoms and collide with them. Summer 2023 examiners saw many answers lose this mark by naming a particle from inside the atom.

parts.stem:
The toaster has a power of 0.92 kW and is connected to the 230 V mains.
Calculate the current in the element.
hints: Write P = I × V first. The power must be in watts before it goes in.

commonErrors.feedback: The power went in as 0.92, still in kilowatts, so the current is 1000 times too small. Convert first: 0.92 kW = 920 W, then I = 920 ÷ 230 = 4 A. Summer 2023 examiners saw marks lost here to the kilowatt conversion.

That divides the voltage by the power, which is P = I × V rearranged upside down. The current is the power divided by the voltage: 920 ÷ 230 = 4 A. A toaster drawing a quarter of an amp would barely warm up; a few amps is what a kitchen appliance takes.

parts.stem:
A student investigates the link between the length of a wire and its resistance. The resistance is found from the readings on two meters, X and Y.
Choose the name of each meter.

scheme.for: Y: ammeter, in series with the wire
X: voltmeter, in parallel with (across) the length being tested

hints: Follow each meter's leads: one meter has the whole current flowing through it, the other is joined to the two clips.
parts.workedSolution: Y is the ammeter: it sits in the main loop, in series, so the current in the wire flows through it. X is the voltmeter: its two leads go to the two clips, so it is in parallel with the length being tested.

commonErrors.feedback: The two meters have been swapped. The meter in the main loop, Y, has the current flowing through it, so it is the ammeter; the meter joined to the two clips, X, is across the wire, so it is the voltmeter. Summer 2025 examiners saw many answers put the meters in the wrong places and lose both marks.

parts.stem: Name one controlled variable for this investigation.

scheme.for: temperature / material / cross-sectional area (thickness) of the wire
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Booklet B Foundation: the hardest part of the paper; most candidates wrote the length of the wire.

hints: Name the three variables in order: the one changed, the one measured, then what must stay the same.
parts.workedSolution: Any one of the temperature, the material or the thickness (cross-sectional area) of the wire. Each of them would change the resistance if it changed, so each is kept the same.

commonErrors.feedback: The length is the variable being changed, the independent variable, so it cannot also be kept the same. What must stay the same is something else about the wire: its temperature, its material or its thickness. Summer 2025 examiners found most candidates gave the length here.

The results are in the table.
Plot the five results on the grid, and draw a straight line of best fit.

scheme.for: three points plotted correctly, each within half a small square
at least four points plotted correctly
one ruled straight line of best fit

hints: Each row of the table is one point: the length across, the resistance up.
Lay one ruled line through the points; do not join them dot to dot.
parts.workedSolution: The points are (0.2, 2.2), (0.4, 4.4), (0.6, 6.6), (0.8, 8.8), (1.0, 11.0), and one ruled straight line passes through all five and the origin. On the paper the grid's scale (using at least half of it) and the label resistance / Ω earn two more marks, [5] in all.

parts.stem: State how the resistance of the wire is related to its length.

accepted: resistance is directly proportional to length

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 Booklet B Foundation: poorly answered; most tried an explanation in their own words, which gained nothing.

hints: Your line is straight and passes through the origin. There is one scientific term for that.
parts.workedSolution: Resistance is directly proportional to length: the graph is a straight line through the origin.

commonErrors.feedback: That describes the trend in your own words, which gains nothing here. A straight line through the origin has one scientific term: resistance is directly proportional to length.

questions.solutionProgram: points (0.2, 2.2) (0.4, 4.4) (0.6, 6.6) (0.8, 8.8) (1, 11); each R = 11 * L, so the line of best fit is R = 11 L through the origin

figures.alt: A graph on a grid of resistance in ohms, 0 to 12, against length of wire in metres, 0 to 1.2, with the five results plotted as crosses and a ruled straight line of best fit through the origin.

parts.stem:
A student measures the voltage across five lengths of one wire, with the current kept at 0.20 A for every reading. The resistance for 0.60 m is missing from the table.
Calculate it.
hints: Resistance = voltage ÷ current, using that row's voltage and the current in the question.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the voltage by the current. Resistance is voltage divided by current: 1.08 ÷ 0.20 = 5.4 Ω.
That is current ÷ voltage, the equation upside down. R = V ÷ I = 1.08 ÷ 0.20 = 5.4 Ω.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the student's results plotted with a line of best fit.
State what the graph shows about the resistance and the length of the wire.

accepted: resistance is directly proportional to length

hints: The line is straight and goes through the origin.
parts.workedSolution: Resistance is directly proportional to length: the line of best fit is straight and passes through the origin.

commonErrors.feedback: True, but it is the trend in your own words. The mark needs the term: resistance is directly proportional to length.

parts.stem: Calculate the gradient of the line of best fit.

scheme.for: correct values read from a large triangle on the line, e.g. 9.0 ÷ 1.0

hints: Use the line, not the table: pick two points on the line far apart.
The line passes through the origin, so one corner of the triangle can be (0, 0).
parts.workedSolution:
gradient = rise ÷ run
gradient = 9.0 ÷ 1.0
gradient = 9.0
The triangle runs from the origin to the point on the line at 1.0 m.

parts.stem: Give the unit of the gradient.
hints: The unit up the side divided by the unit along the bottom.
parts.workedSolution: Ω/m, ohms per metre.

commonErrors.feedback: Ohms alone is the unit of resistance. The gradient is ohms divided by metres: Ω/m. Summer 2025 Higher examiners saw a surprising number miss this.

parts.stem: Use the gradient to calculate the resistance of 2.5 m of the same wire.
hints: The gradient is the resistance of one metre.
parts.workedSolution: 9.0 Ω for every metre, so 2.5 m has 9.0 × 2.5 = 22.5 Ω.

questions.solutionProgram: R = 1.08 / 0.2 = 5.4; least-squares gradient through the origin = 8.991 ~ 9; R(2.5) = 9 * 2.5 = 22.5

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciarán is asked: 'At a length of 0.80 m the voltmeter reads 2.0 V and the ammeter reads 400 mA. Calculate the resistance of this length of wire. [3]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 divides by 400, which is the current in milliamps. The equation needs amperes: 400 mA ÷ 1000 = 0.40 A. Dividing by a number 1000 times too big makes the resistance 1000 times too small.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three, for the equation. A resistance of a few thousandths of an ohm for a length of lab wire should look wrong, and checking the unit on the ammeter reading catches it. Summer 2025 Higher examiners saw a significant minority lose marks by not converting milliamps to amperes in an Ohm's law calculation.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'At a length of 0.60 m the voltmeter reads 2.5 V and the ammeter reads 0.25 A. Calculate the resistance of this length of wire. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 has the equation upside down. Resistance is the voltage it takes to push each ampere through, so it is voltage divided by current: R = V ÷ I. Every line after it follows the wrong equation, so the answer is the reciprocal of the right one.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks of three: the equation mark is lost, and the substitution and answer followed the wrong equation, so they earn nothing either. Summer 2024 examiners saw many start from an incorrect version of R = V/I and score zero. A lab wire of about 10 Ω is sensible; a fraction of an ohm for 0.60 m of resistance wire should look wrong.

prompts.prompt: Why does a metal wire get hot when a current flows through it?
prompts.answer: Free electrons collide with the metal atoms and give them energy, so the atoms vibrate more: that is heat.

prompts.prompt: For one wire at a constant temperature, how does its resistance depend on its length?
prompts.answer: Resistance is directly proportional to length: double the length, double the resistance.

prompts.prompt: Which two features of a graph show that two quantities are directly proportional?
prompts.answer: It is a straight line, and it passes through the origin.

prompts.prompt: Name the control variables in the resistance and length practical.
prompts.answer: The thickness, the material and the temperature of the wire. The length is the one you change.

prompts.prompt: What is the unit of the gradient of a graph of resistance (Ω) against length (m)?
prompts.answer: Ohms per metre, Ω/m: the gradient is the resistance of one metre of the wire.

prompts.prompt: Where do the ammeter and the voltmeter go in the resistance and length practical?
prompts.answer: The ammeter in series with the wire; the voltmeter across the length being tested.

prompts.prompt: Why is the current switched off between readings in the resistance and length practical?
prompts.answer: So the wire does not heat up, because a hotter wire has a higher resistance.
